newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk generals mount campaign to rein in Islamists.
newsitem.headline: Turk generals mount campaign to rein in Islamists.

text.p: Turkey's secularist generals have mounted a "soft coup" against the republic's first Islamist leader, ordering him to crack down on religious radicalism and sparing any need for tanks in the streets, analysts said.
Top force commanders at the weekend directed Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan to choke off the religious revival that has underpinned the rise of his Islam-based Welfare Party.

The restive army brass also named one of their own to monitor compliance in what is essentially a forced reassertion of the secularist values of state founder -- and creator of the modern Turkish army -- Kemal Ataturk.
"This is a soft coup, a more convenient version...of (earlier) coups, better suited to modern times," political commentator Bilal Cetin told Reuters.
"There is a pseudo-civilian government and a military wing to give them directives," he said.
Analysts said the soft approach was calculated to avoid the international condemnation that would surely accompany any direct army intervention.

The military-dominated National Security Council, a holdover from army rule in the early 1960s, demanded Erbakan limit religious training, restrict the often-secretive Islamic brotherhoods, or tarikats, and enforce bans on Islamic dress.
Other steps include investigations of Islamist-owned businesses -- a key source of the Welfare Party's funding -- and ending grants to Turkish students abroad who engage in Islamist agitation.
Erbakan sought to give the impression of business as usual.
"In Turkey governments are formed in parliament, not in the National Security Council (NSC). Laws are made in parliament," he told a news conference.
However, the NSC directives call for enforcement of existing laws, some dating back to the foundation of the secular republic seven decades ago.
As if to underscore the military's determination, a senior commander was widely quoted on Monday as dismissing Erbakan's assertion at the weekend that he was in harmony with the army.

The generals' political assault follows months of tension between the Islamists and Turkey's pro-Western secularists, backed up by the armed forces. Nightly protests against state corruption have increasingly targetted Erbakan and Welfare.

At issue are a series of Islam-based initiatives, including the construction of mosque in secular strongholds, lifting the ban on Islamic headscarves in government workplaces and an eastward "turn" in NATO-member Turkey's foreign policy.
Already the soldiers have brought down three civilian governments -- in 1960, 1971 and 1980 -- and few doubt they would do so again if they saw a threat to the secular order.
"The National Security Council decision looks more like a beginning than an end," columnist Fikret Bila wrote in the liberal Milliyet daily.
"The NSC will monitor the government. From the perspective of the government there is a type of 'custody'...The military wants results."

It is precisely this army-imposed yardstick that holds the greatest danger for Erbakan, threatening to make him the instrument of an anti-Islamist campaign and undoing decades of dogged campaigning on behalf of traditional religious values.
The only other choices, say analysts, may be resignation or collapse of his coalition with a pro-Western conservative party.

"It is history's great irony that it is the Welfare Party that must implement these measures" and return the country to the secular path of Ataturk, said commentator Ismet Berkan in the daily Radikal.
"Was it not Erbakan who said that if Ataturk were alive today he would join the Welfare Party? Of course it was. And now Erbakan has the chance to become Ataturk II."

As the army and Erbakan slug it out, many lament the failure of Turkish politics to produce an alternative to the coalition led by Welfare, which received just 21 percent of the vote in general elections in December of 1995.

"The politicians have left a gap and what should have been discussed under normal condition inside parliament were (instead) covered by the NSC," said Mehmet Ali Birand, a columnist and leading authority on Turkey's coups.
"This is what must be called 'Turkish-style democracy,'" he said.
